title: Attention Is All You Need
field: machine learning and natural language processing
paragraphs: Some computer programs work with words in a row. The words have an order. One word comes after the next. They use what came before to help with what comes next. For example, they can read a line of text, one word at a time. They do not look at just one word on its own. They can use the words they have seen to help guess the next word. A word near the start can help with a word near the end. Some of these programs are among the best at this work. They can learn how words fit together. They can also change words from one language to another. The new words can say the same thing in a new way. People keep trying to make these programs better. They also work on systems that take words in and give new words back. These systems can help with the same kinds of work.

This helps it handle what comes next. It keeps track of earlier parts as it moves through the words. For example, a model might look at earlier words to help guess the next word. The words already seen give it clues about what might follow. This can help it learn how words fit together. These models have become leading tools for learning patterns in language and translating text from one language to another. Certain kinds are especially good at keeping track of earlier words. Recurrent neural networks are computer models that work with sequences, such as strings of words. They use what came earlier to help with what comes next. A sequence has an order, so changing that order can change what it means. For example, a model can use earlier words in a sentence to help predict a later word. In a language model, the words already seen provide context for a prediction. These networks are leading tools for learning language patterns and translating text. Long short-term memory networks are one well-known type. Researchers keep working to make these language models better. They also improve encoder-decoder systems. These take in one sequence and produce another. In an encoder-decoder system, the encoder handles the input, and the decoder produces the output. Such systems can help translate text from one language to another. In translation, the input and output sequences are written in different languages.

Recurrent neural networks, especially long short-term memory and gated recurrent networks, are well-established tools for sequence modeling and transduction. These tasks include language modeling, in which a model learns patterns in sequences of words. A recurrent language model uses earlier elements of a sequence when predicting subsequent elements. The ordering of elements is central to both tasks: changing word order can change the meaning of a sentence. They also include machine translation, which converts text from one language to another. In transduction, a model maps an input sequence to an output sequence. An encoder-decoder architecture can map an input sentence to a sentence in another language. In such a system, the encoder processes the source sequence, and the decoder generates the target sequence using a representation of that input. Researchers have continued to improve recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures, pushing the limits of how well these systems work on sequence tasks.

Some computer models read a row of words one at a time. At each word, the model keeps a note of what it has seen. The note is like a small reminder. It helps the model use what came before. It uses that note and the next word to make a new note. The model makes one note for each new word. Like people in a line, the steps must wait for one another. The next note cannot be made until the last one is done. It cannot skip ahead and fill in a note later. It must go step by step through the row. A long row has more steps, and each one must wait its turn. This can slow learning, more so with long rows, since memory is limited. New tricks help the models learn faster. Some also help them do better. But the steps still have to go in order.

Some computer models work through a string of words one place at a time. At each place, the model uses the new word and what it saved from the last step. It uses both to update what it knows. The saved information passes from one step to the next. The steps depend on one another, so they cannot all run at once. That is why the model cannot make all its updates at the same time. For a long string, there are more steps to finish in turn. The model must wait for each update before it makes the next one. Long strings make this a bigger problem, because computer memory limits how many examples can be grouped. It can group separate examples, but there is only so much room in memory for them. New methods speed up training, and some improve results. But the steps still run in order.

Recurrent models process a sequence, such as a series of words, one position at a time. At each step, the model uses the current input and a hidden state, a record of past steps, to produce a new state. The hidden state carries information forward from one position to the next. Each step must wait for the one before it, so the steps cannot run in parallel. That means the model cannot prepare a later state until it has produced the earlier one. Even if the computer has resources for several operations at once, it must first have the state needed for the next step. Longer sequences therefore require more of these dependent steps. Long sequences make this a problem, since memory limits how many examples can run at once. It can still process separate examples together, within memory limits. New methods speed up the work, and some improve results, but the steps still run in order.

Recurrent models process input and output sequences one position at a time. At each step, the model uses the current input and the previous hidden state to create a new state. The hidden state carries information forward through the sequence, linking the computation at each position to the one before it. This chain of steps cannot run in parallel within a training example. The dependence between successive states means that processing a later position requires the state produced at the preceding position. Adding more hardware cannot remove that dependence. Long sequences make the limit more serious, since memory limits how many examples can be grouped at once. Separate training examples can still be processed together, but the amount of available memory limits the size of such a batch. New methods use factorization or conditional computation to speed up the work; the latter can also improve results, but the steps must still run in order.

Recurrent models divide computation across positions in input and output sequences. At each position, they generate a hidden state $h_t$ from the previous state $h_{t-1}$ and the input at position $t$. Each state must be ready before the next one can be computed, making the work sequential and preventing parallel processing of positions within a training example. The constraint is especially serious for long sequences, which require more steps in this chain. A model can still process separate examples in parallel by grouping them into a batch. However, memory limits how many examples can fit in a batch, particularly when sequences are long. Recent work has used factorization tricks and conditional computation to make these models more efficient. Conditional computation can also improve model performance by choosing which operations to perform. Yet these advances do not remove the basic need to compute the states in order, even when more processing power is available.

Consequently, even with additional processing resources, the state at a later position must await completion of the computations at earlier positions in the same sequence. This becomes a serious limit for long sequences, as memory constraints restrict batching across examples. Factorization tricks and conditional computation make the work more efficient. The latter can also improve model performance, but the basic constraint of sequential computation remains.

Attention helps a computer work with words. It can link words that are far apart. It can link words near each other too. Think of a long line of words. Some words go together, even if many words lie between them. A computer can use these links to make sense of a line. The words do not have to sit side by side. Most systems use it with a way that takes one step at a time. We offer a new system called the Transformer. It uses attention. But it does not use that step-by-step way. It can do more work at the same time. It can work on many parts of a line at once. It need not work through all the parts one by one. It set a new high mark for changing words from one language to another. It took just twelve hours to train on eight P100 computer chips.

Attention helps a computer find links between parts of a sequence. A sequence is a set of things in order, such as words in a sentence. Words can be linked even when many other words come between them. Attention can find these links, whether the words are near or far apart. This can help a model turn one sequence into another. For example, it can help turn words in one language into words in another. Most models use attention with a network that works through a sequence one step at a time. We propose a new model called the Transformer. It uses attention, but it does not need that step-by-step network. This lets it do more work at the same time. It can work on many parts of a sequence together. After just twelve hours of training on eight P100 chips, it reached a new best level of quality in translation.

For example, two words in a sentence may be connected even when many words lie between them. Attention can find links between nearby parts as well. Most models use it with a network that works through a sequence step by step. We propose the Transformer, which uses attention without that step-by-step network. It can do more work at once. After only twelve hours of training on eight P100 chips, it reached a new best result in translation.

A sequence model handles ordered data, such as words in a sentence. Attention helps a model find links between parts of a sequence, even when they are far apart. For example, a word near the start of a sentence may relate to one near the end. Attention can capture this link without treating the gap as a barrier. In translation, a model turns a sequence in one language into a sequence in another. Attention helps it connect related parts of the input and output. Most models use attention with a recurrent network, which works through a sequence one step at a time. We propose the Transformer, a model that uses attention rather than recurrence to connect input and output. It can do more of its work in parallel, meaning at the same time. After as little as twelve hours of training on eight P100 GPUs, it can reach a new best level of translation quality.

Attention mechanisms help sequence models capture links between elements, even when they are far apart in the input or output. A model can use attention to connect nearby positions as well as those separated by many words. In translation, for example, the input and output are sequences in different languages. Attention can help the model find links within and between these sequences, even when their parts appear in a different order. Most models use attention alongside a recurrent network, which processes a sequence one step at a time. We propose the Transformer, a model that avoids recurrence and relies entirely on attention to connect input and output across the whole sequence. This design allows the model to do much more of its work in parallel, rather than in a fixed series of steps. After as little as twelve hours of training on eight P100 GPUs, it can reach a new state of the art in translation quality.

Attention mechanisms enable sequence models to capture dependencies between elements regardless of their distance in the input or output. We propose the Transformer, an architecture that eliminates recurrence and relies entirely on attention to connect input and output across the sequence. Attention mechanisms are integral to sequence modeling and transduction across a range of tasks, allowing dependencies to be modeled regardless of their distance in input or output sequences. In most cases, however, attention is used in conjunction with a recurrent network. We propose the Transformer, an architecture eschewing recurrence and relying entirely on attention to draw global dependencies between input and output. Without recurrent steps, the model can process more sequence positions in parallel during training. Although autoregressive decoding can still impose sequential steps across output tokens, the attention-based architecture removes recurrent state transitions from the computation of representations. In translation, attention relates positions within the source and target sequences as well as across them. These relationships are not constrained by sequence distance. The Transformer allows significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after as little as twelve hours of training on eight P100 GPUs.

Some computer models can work on many words at once instead of handling them one by one. A sentence can have words that depend on one another even when other words lie between them. But they need more steps to connect words that are farther apart. That makes it harder for them to learn how distant words relate. For example, a word at the start of a sentence may be linked to one near the end. The gap between them can make the link harder to learn. The models must still find those links to make sense of the sentence. The Transformer uses the same number of steps to connect any two words. It combines what it finds, which can blur some details. We have it pay attention in several ways at once to help make up for this loss. Each way can focus on different words and pick up different details.

Several neural network models process all positions in a sequence at the same time. A sequence might be a sentence, with each word at a position. They do not have to work through them one by one. But connecting two positions takes more operations as the distance between them grows. This makes distant relationships harder to learn. For example, a word near the beginning of a sentence may relate to one near the end. In these earlier models, information must pass through more steps to make such a connection. The extra steps can make long-range links more difficult to learn. Such links can help a model understand how the parts fit together. The Transformer uses a fixed number of operations to connect any two positions. It averages information from the positions it attends to, which can blur distinctions. We use multiple attention heads, which attend in different ways, to help offset that loss. Each head can focus on different positions, giving the model several views of the sequence.

Convolutional networks compute representations for all positions in a sequence at once. These models aim to reduce sequential computation, so positions need not be processed one after another. But they need more operations to link positions that are farther apart. For ConvS2S, the number of operations grows in direct proportion to distance. For ByteNet, it grows more slowly, at a logarithmic rate. A linear increase tracks the size of the gap, while a logarithmic increase rises more slowly as that gap expands. In either case, the path between positions grows longer as they move apart. Links across greater distances thus require more stages of computation. This makes distant dependencies harder to learn. The Transformer uses a fixed number of operations for any two positions. Its attention averages information across positions, which can blur details. We use Multi-Head Attention to help offset this loss. Each head can focus on different positions, giving the model more than one view of the sequence.

The Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet and ConvS2S use convolutional networks to compute hidden representations at all input and output positions in parallel. This design reduces sequential computation by allowing positions to be processed simultaneously. Yet more operations are needed to link positions that are far apart. For ConvS2S, the number of operations grows linearly with distance. For ByteNet, it grows logarithmically. A linear increase means that doubling the separation roughly doubles the path length, whereas a logarithmic increase makes the path grow much more slowly as that separation increases. These scaling properties concern the operations needed to connect two positions, not the total computational cost of the models. This makes distant dependencies harder to learn. The resulting distance-dependent paths can make it harder to capture long-range relationships. The Transformer links any two positions in a constant number of operations, but averages attention-weighted positions, reducing effective resolution. We counteract this loss with Multi-Head Attention, as described in Section 3.2.

Self-attention, also called intra-attention, links positions in a single sequence to form a representation of it. It lets a model draw on other parts of the same sequence when encoding each position. The sequence may consist of words or other ordered input units, and the representation can capture relationships among them. These links can connect positions that are far apart as well as those that are close together. Self-attention has been used for reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment, and learning sentence representations that work across tasks. In abstractive summarization, the output can express the source content in new wording rather than merely extract passages. End-to-end memory networks use recurrent attention rather than recurrence aligned with sequence positions. In these networks, attention is applied repeatedly without tying each step to a position in the sequence. Recurrent attention allows the network to consult its memory over multiple steps. They have performed well on simple-language question answering and language modeling.

Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention, is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence to compute a representation of that sequence. Unlike attention between separate sequences, it derives relationships from positions within the same sequence. These relationships can span many intervening elements. Self-attention has been used successfully in reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations. Such representations are intended for use across tasks. They need not be restricted to the task on which they were learned. In abstractive summarization, the generated summary may employ wording not present in the source. Textual entailment concerns whether one statement follows from another. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence-aligned recurrence. They repeatedly attend to memory over computational steps, rather than associating each recurrent step with a successive position in the input sequence. These networks have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks.

An attention tool helps pick what to use. It starts with a query, or what we want to find. It also gets pairs of keys and values. Each key goes with one value. These pairs are given to the tool along with the query. They help it work out what to use. Think of a key as a label on a box. The value is what is in the box. The tool uses the label to choose how much of what is inside to use. The tool checks how well the query fits each key. A close fit gives that key’s value more weight. A poor fit gives it less. Then the tool blends the values, using those weights, to make an output. The query, keys, values, and output are all groups of numbers. The end result is one new group of numbers. It is made from the values, not from the keys or the query.

A big key has more numbers than a small key. With a small key, both ways work about as well. With a big key, the add way works better if we do not shrink the dot way’s scores. A score is a number that helps the model decide what to pay attention to. With a big key, a dot score can be very far from zero. We think such scores can make the next step give the model a very weak signal for learning.[^4] That is like a voice too faint to hear. To help with this, we shrink the dot scores before the next step. We shrink them more when the key is bigger. This helps the model learn from those scores.

We use two methods to help a model focus on information. We call one the adding method and the other the dot method. Each uses a key, or group of numbers. A larger key contains more numbers, which the dot method uses to calculate a score. The score helps the model decide how much attention to give to information. Attention helps a model focus on useful information, and we compare two types: additive attention and dot-product attention. When the key size is small, both work about equally well. When the key size is large, additive attention works better if the dot products are not scaled down. A larger key has more components, so the dot product combines more pairs of numbers. The dot product is a score made by multiplying matching numbers and adding the results. With more components, that score can grow in size. We think large dot products make the softmax function give very weak signals for learning.[^4] Softmax turns scores into weights that guide the model’s focus. If the learning signals become too weak, it becomes harder to adjust the model’s weights during training. To fix this, we scale down the dot products. Scaling reduces the resulting score before softmax turns it into a weight.

When the key dimension $d_k$ is small, additive attention and dot-product attention work about equally well. At larger values of $d_k$, additive attention works better than dot-product attention without scaling. The dot product combines corresponding parts of a query and a key to produce a score. We suspect that large dot products push the softmax function into regions where its gradients are extremely small.[^4] Softmax turns scores into attention weights, and the gradients guide the model’s learning during training. The problem is not simply that a score is large, but that softmax can become too insensitive to changes in its inputs. In that regime, even a useful adjustment to a score may produce only a very small change in the weights. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ before applying softmax. Scaling reduces the size of that score without changing its sign. This helps keep the gradients from becoming too small.

For small values of $d_k$, additive and dot-product attention perform similarly, but additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention at larger values. The dot product sums the products of corresponding query and key components, so its magnitude can increase with the number of dimensions. We suspect that, as $d_k$ increases, dot products grow large in magnitude and push the softmax function into regions where its gradients are extremely small.[^4] In a saturated softmax, attention weights can become concentrated on a single input, and small changes in the scores produce correspondingly small changes in those weights. Because these gradients carry the learning signal back through the attention mechanism, their reduction can hinder learning. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ before applying softmax. Scaling moderates the scores presented to softmax. Scaling does not remove the differences between scores, but changes the range presented to the function.

We found a way to help a model look at things. It takes more than one look at the same time. Each look uses its own way that the model has learned. The model learns how to make each look. The looks all work at the same time. They do not have to take turns. Each can pick out things in different places. Each one can find a part of what is there. A look can find one bit while the next finds a different bit. Think of two kids who look at a game. Each kid may see something the other kid did not. Then we join what the looks find. We change that mix to get the final result. The model can use both bits when it makes its last result. This lets the model see more than one kind of detail at once. With just one look, details can blend together.

We found that a model can do better if it uses several ways to focus at once. Each way learns to look at the same input in a different way. These ways work at the same time, not one after another. Each uses what it has learned to change the input before it looks for details. It can pick out different details from different places. The model then joins what each way finds. It changes the mix to make one final result. This is like asking a few people to look at a picture and share what they see. Each person might notice a detail that the others miss. In the same way, each learned way can give the model a different view. Joining the results lets the model use those views together, instead of relying on just one view of the input. With just one way to focus, some details can blur together.

We found that a model performs better with several attention heads than with one. Each head learns its own way to change three inputs: queries, keys, and values. Queries and keys help the model choose where to focus. Values carry the information it uses. Each head uses its own learned changes to form a different view of the inputs. Its attention result combines values according to how well queries and keys match. The heads work at the same time, and we combine and change their outputs to get the final result. For example, one head might focus on a nearby word, while another focuses on a word farther away. Each head can also use a different view of the information at those positions. The final result brings these separate attention results together. This lets the model focus on different kinds of information at different positions. A single head can blur these differences by averaging them.

We found it helpful to use multiple attention heads rather than a single attention function, with each head using learned linear projections to change the queries, keys, and values. The heads then compute attention in parallel, each using its own set of changed inputs; we join their outputs and project them again to get the final values. Each head can therefore produce a different weighted combination of values from the same inputs. The final projection brings the joined results back into a form the model can use. For example, one head may focus on a nearby word, while another attends to a word farther away. Because the projections are learned separately, the heads can also draw on different features of the input when they compute their attention results. This lets the model attend to distinct kinds of information at different positions. With a single head, averaging can blur these differences.

We found it useful to use separate learned linear projections of queries, keys and values for multiple attention heads. Each head maps these inputs to $d_k$, $d_k$ and $d_v$ dimensions, respectively. Because each head has its own projection matrices, it can represent the same inputs differently before attention is computed. The learned projections give each head its own representation of the queries, keys and values, rather than requiring all heads to share one representation. The heads then compute attention in parallel. Parallel computation produces separate weighted combinations of values, which the final projection can combine across heads. We concatenate the resulting $d_v$-dimensional outputs and project them again to obtain the final values. The concatenation preserves the separate head outputs until the final projection. This allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, while averaging within a single head limits this ability.

Instead of performing a single attention function with $d_{\mathrm{model}}$-dimensional keys, values and queries, we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values $h$ times with different, learned linear projections to $d_k$, $d_k$ and $d_v$ dimensions, respectively. On each of these projected versions of queries, keys and values we then perform the attention function in parallel, yielding $d_v$-dimensional output values. Each head therefore applies the attention function to a distinct set of learned projections, rather than sharing a single projection of the inputs. These are concatenated and once again linearly projected, resulting in the final output values, as depicted in Figure 2. Concatenation retains the individual outputs as components of the combined representation, which is then transformed by the final projection. Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

We use eight small heads at the same time. A head is a part of the model that helps it find things in what it reads. We use sets of numbers to shape what each head looks for and what it sends on. Each head uses 64 numbers to help find things. It uses 64 more to hold what it finds. The heads can look at different parts of the text. They all do this at the same time, like a team working on a task. Each one sends back what it finds. We join what the heads send on. Then we use one more set of numbers to shape it. This gives the model one result to use in its next step. The model learns these sets of numbers as it trains. All eight heads take about as much work as one big head. That is because each small head works with fewer numbers. So using more heads does not mean doing eight times the work.

We use eight attention heads in parallel, meaning that they work at the same time. Each head uses learned sets of numbers to transform queries, keys and values, the signals that help the model find and pass along information. These sets of numbers are learned during training, and each head has its own. For each head, the transformed queries, keys and values each have 64 numbers. The model compares queries with keys to decide which values to use. Each head then produces a result from those values. We join the results from all eight heads and transform them again to produce a single output. This gives the model a result it can use in the next step. Because each head works with fewer numbers, the total computing cost is similar to that of one head using the full model size. Thus, eight heads can work together without needing eight times as much computing.

We use eight attention heads in parallel, each with its own learned projections of queries, keys and values. These projections transform the input into vectors, or ordered sets of numbers, for each head. The projection for each type of input has parameters that the model learns during training. Different heads can therefore learn different ways to represent the same input before computing attention. For every head, the key, query and value vectors each have 64 dimensions. A query is compared with keys to determine how much weight to give the associated values. Each head uses those weights to produce its own output. The resulting outputs are joined before the final projection. We also apply a separate projection to the combined output from all eight heads. This final projection returns the joined result to the model’s full representation size. Because each head uses a reduced number of dimensions, the overall computational cost is similar to that of a single full-size attention head. The benefit of multiple heads thus comes without an eightfold increase in computation.

The first part keeps what it has read. The second part sends a question about what it needs. The first part supplies clues from the input. The second part can ask about that whole line. This lets the output part look at the whole input at each spot. Each spot in its new line can use the clues. It can use clues from any spot in that input. It does not have to look at just one word. It can look back at all the words in the line. Each view can help it find clues. Other tools that turn one line into another work in much the same way.

The part of the model that reads the input works in steps. Some steps let it look back at the step just before. At each spot, it can look at every spot in that last step. To do this, it uses three sets of things from that same step. One set helps it ask what to look for. The other two help it find and use what is there. All three sets come from what the last step made. It can look at the first spot, the last spot, or one in the middle. It can look at them all, not just the ones close by. It can use what it finds at those spots to help make the next step. It does not need to look only at the spot right next to it. The three sets all start with the same last step. That is how it can look across the whole input.

The encoder is the part of the model that reads the input. It has layers, or steps, that change the input. Some of these layers use self-attention. This means that each place in a layer can look at every place in the layer before it. To do this, it uses three sets of information. These are called queries, keys and values. All three sets come from the same place: the output of the previous encoder layer. For example, a place near the start can look at a place near the end. It can also use information from places in between. It is not limited to its neighbors. At each place, a query can be matched with keys from all the places in the previous layer. The layer can then use values from those places to build its output. This gives each place a way to draw on the whole input, not just a small part of it.

Our model makes an answer one step at a time. At each step, it can look at that step and all the steps before it. But it must not look at steps that come later. That would be like seeing the last page of a story too soon. Think of writing a tale from the start. You can read what you have put down so far. You cannot read what you have not yet written. Each new step comes after the last one. We block links to later steps before the model picks what to look at. For each step, we make a new set of links. Some links lead back, and one stays at that step. The rest lead ahead. We shut off those links, so they play no part in what the model does next. This helps it make each new part using only what comes first. See Figure 2.

In the decoder, self-attention allows each position to attend to itself and all earlier positions, but not to later ones. This restriction preserves the auto-regressive property by preventing information from future positions from flowing leftward. We enforce it in scaled dot-product attention by masking the softmax inputs for illegal connections: we set those values to $-\infty$ before computing the attention weights. The masked entries contribute zero attention weight after softmax, while the weights of the permitted connections are normalized over the current and earlier positions. This constraint applies at every decoder position. For a given query position, the set of permitted keys therefore grows with its position in the sequence. The mask is applied before normalization, so forbidden entries receive no probability mass and cannot affect the weighted sum of values. Thus, each position can use only the current position and the preceding part of the decoder sequence. See Figure 2.

Our model has two main parts. Each part has layers. We use both parts to work with a string of data. A spot is one place in that string. Each layer pays attention to the data. Each layer also has a small network. This network works on each spot on its own. It uses the same steps at each spot. But its settings differ from one layer to the next. At each spot, it does one step, then changes values below zero to zero, then does a second step. We can think of the two steps as two passes with a one-spot window. The window looks at just one spot at a time. It does not look at the next spot when it works on one spot. It uses the same steps, but not the same data, at each spot. The input and output have 512 values; the middle has 2048. The middle is four times as wide.

We teach our model to turn word pieces it reads and makes into lists of numbers. A word piece can be a whole word or part of one. Each list has the same size. A list is like a row of boxes. Each box holds a number. The model can use the lists to work with the text. Then we use what the model has worked out to guess the next word piece. We use the same set of numbers to make both kinds of lists and to help make the guess. The model learns the numbers as it trains. It uses the same set in more than one place. It does not need a new set for each job. When we make the lists, we first make those numbers larger by an amount tied to the list size. The guess gives a chance for each next piece. The chances all add up to one.

We train our model to turn tokens into lists of numbers. Tokens are pieces of text, either fed in or produced as output. A token can be a whole word or just part of one. All of these lists have the same length. The list lets the model work with that token as numbers. We use the model’s output to work out the chance of each possible next token. The chances for all the possible next tokens add up to one. The same table of learned numbers helps make both kinds of lists and the next-token chances. This table is learned during training, rather than fixed by hand. Using it in more than one place means that the model does not need a separate table for each of these jobs. Each dimension of a positional encoding follows a sinusoidal wave, with wavelengths increasing by a fixed ratio from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$. A fixed ratio means that each wavelength is obtained by multiplying the previous one by the same factor. Here $pos$ is a position in the sequence, and $i$ identifies a dimension of its encoding. The wavelengths span a wide range, giving different dimensions waves at different frequencies. We thought that this pattern would help the model learn to attend to relative positions. For any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. The same linear relationship holds across starting positions for a given offset, giving the model a way to connect positions by their separation. We also tested learned positional embeddings, which produced nearly identical results. We chose the sinusoidal version because it may work on sequences longer than those seen during training. This potential to handle longer inputs is a reason for the choice, not a guarantee of success.

The progression therefore supplies position signals that vary over both short and long scales. We hypothesized that this function would help the model learn attention based on relative positions, since for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. For a given displacement, this relationship applies regardless of the starting position, providing a basis for position-dependent attention. We also tested learned positional embeddings and found nearly identical results (Table 3 row (E)). We chose the sinusoidal version because it may generalize to sequences longer than those encountered during training. The sinusoidal function also defines encodings beyond the training range, although the ability to extrapolate is not guaranteed.

We look at ways a computer can change a list of things. Each way makes a new list with the same number of things. For each way, the list can be short or long. But the new list has just as many things as the old one. Think of a row of cards. A new row comes out with one card for each card in the first row. One way looks at how things in the list relate to each other. We compare it with two other ways. We ask how much work each way takes. We also ask how much work can be done at once. To find that out, we count the steps that must come one after the other. Some jobs can be done at the same time. Others must wait for a step to end before the next step can start. These are two of three things we look at.

We compare three types of layers that change sequences, or lists of symbols in order. Each layer makes an output sequence as long as its input. The input can be short or long, and the output has the same number of positions. For example, the input might represent words in a sentence, while the output holds a new representation for each position. These layers can be part of a model that processes sequences. A self-attention layer links each position to others in the sequence. A recurrent layer works through positions in order. A convolutional layer looks at small groups of positions. To explain our use of self-attention, we use three measures. Two are the total work per layer and the fewest steps that must run one after another. Some operations can happen at the same time, but others must wait for an earlier operation to finish.

We compare self-attention layers with recurrent and convolutional layers. These are common ways to transform a sequence of symbol representations into a new sequence of the same length. The input can vary in length, but each input position has a corresponding position in the output. For example, the input may represent the words in a sentence, and the output assigns a new representation to each position. This comparison focuses on the work within each layer. Such layers can be used in an encoder or decoder. To explain our use of self-attention, we consider three criteria. One is the total computational work each layer requires. Another is how much of that work can be done in parallel, measured by the fewest operations that must happen one after another. Parallel work can happen at the same time, while sequential operations must wait for earlier operations to finish. These measures describe different aspects of the cost.

The third factor we compare is the path length between distant positions in a network. Learning long-range dependencies, or links between elements far apart, is a key challenge in tasks that transform one sequence into another. For example, a word near the beginning of a sentence may be related to another word much later in the sentence. The ability to learn these links depends in part on the paths that forward and backward signals must travel. The distance between words in a sequence need not match the length of the path through the network: different layer types connect positions in different ways. Shorter paths between input and output positions make such links easier to learn. We therefore compare the longest path between any input and output positions across different types of network layers. This maximum captures the longest such route, rather than the route for a particular pair. It allows us to compare how readily different network designs can support connections across a sequence.

One way to link words looks at them all at once. A list can be a row of words. It takes the same number of steps in a row, no matter how long the list is. The words can be far apart. They can still be linked. A word at the start can link to one at the end. The link can cross the whole list in one step. Another way takes one step per word. The other way goes in order, one word at a time. The first way can be faster when the list is shorter than the set of numbers used for each word. For very long lists, it could look just at words close by. That may save work, but it makes some paths longer. With the last idea, words far apart may need more steps to reach each other. We plan to test this idea.

Self-attention connects all positions in a fixed number of sequential operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires $O(n)$ operations in sequence. Thus, a position can attend directly to any other position, regardless of their separation in the sequence. The sequential step count for self-attention remains constant as sequence length grows, unlike that of recurrence. In contrast, recurrent computation proceeds sequentially through the positions. Self-attention has lower computational complexity when sequence length $n$ is less than representation dimension $d$, as is often true in machine translation. Sentence representations in translation models often use word pieces or byte-pair units as sequence elements. For very long sequences, we could limit attention to a neighborhood of size $r$ around each output position. This could reduce computation, but it would increase the maximum path length to $O(n/r)$. Restricting the neighborhood limits these direct connections, so information between distant positions must traverse a longer path. We plan to study this approach further.

We need more layers to make all those links. A stack is like steps on a path. That makes paths through the model longer. More steps make the path longer. These layers can take more work than steps that use what came before. We can split the work to cut the cost. But when the group is as wide as the input, this still costs as much as the two steps we use. One step lets each word look at the other words. The next step works on each place on its own. We use both steps in our model. They help the model work with the words it gets.

A convolutional layer looks at a group of input positions at a time. Think of the group as a window that moves across the input. If the window is too narrow, one layer cannot connect every input position to every output position. We need a stack of layers to make all those links. Each layer lets information reach farther, but the paths through the model get longer. Some windows cover positions next to each other. Others skip positions, so they can reach farther in one step. The number of layers needed depends on the width and kind of window. Convolutional layers usually cost more than recurrent layers, which process inputs one at a time. A separable convolution splits the work and costs less. Even when its window is as wide as the input, it costs as much as the two layers we use together. One is a self-attention layer, which connects positions. The other is a feed-forward layer, which works on each position by itself.

A convolutional layer scans the input with a kernel, or window. If the window is narrower than the input, one layer cannot link every input position to every output position. A stack of layers makes those links, but also makes paths through the network longer. The number of layers needed depends on the size and type of kernel. Contiguous kernels cover positions side by side, while dilated kernels skip positions so each layer can reach farther. Convolutional layers generally cost $k$ times as much as recurrent layers, where $k$ is the kernel width. Separable convolutions split the work to reduce the cost. Even when $k = n$, the full input length, their cost matches that of the self-attention and point-wise feed-forward layers we use together in our model. Self-attention lets positions share information across the input, while the feed-forward layer acts on each position on its own in a separate step.

A single convolutional layer with kernel width $k < n$ cannot connect all input and output positions. Full connectivity requires $O(n/k)$ layers with contiguous kernels or $O(\log_k(n))$ with dilated kernels, increasing the longest paths between positions. The required depth depends on both the sequence length and the kernel width, while dilation allows each kernel to span a wider range of positions. In a dilated convolution, sampled input positions are spaced apart rather than adjacent, so the receptive field can grow faster with depth when dilation rates are chosen appropriately. Convolutional layers generally cost $k$ times as much as recurrent layers. Separable convolutions reduce complexity to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$. The separable form reduces computational cost by factoring the convolution into simpler operations. Even with $k = n$, this equals the cost of the self-attention and point-wise feed-forward layers we use together in our model. The comparison assumes the same input and representation dimensions.

A single convolutional layer with kernel width $k < n$ does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of $O(n/k)$ convolutional layers for contiguous kernels, or $O(\log_k(n))$ layers for dilated convolutions. This increases the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. In the contiguous case, successive layers extend the receptive field locally, whereas appropriately chosen dilation rates can expand its span more rapidly, making the connectivity requirement dependent on both kernel width and sampling configuration. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of $k$. Separable convolutions, however, decrease the complexity considerably, to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$. Even with $k = n$, however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model.

We can look at these links for more than one word. Then we can see what each part seems to do. This gives us a peek at its work. We show and talk about some cases at the end of our work. Parts of the tool seem to do different jobs. Some seem to pick up on how words fit together and what they mean. This could make the tool less hard to understand.

Self-attention lets a model use words in a sentence to make sense of other words. It may also make the model easier to understand. We look at which words our models pay attention to. For a given word, we can see which other words get more attention. Such examples can show us the different patterns that the heads learn. A head can give more weight to one word than to another. We can compare its pattern with those of other heads. This lets us see how each head deals with the words, though it does not show us everything the model does. We show and discuss examples at the end of our paper. Parts of the model, called attention heads, clearly learn different jobs. Many seem to notice how words fit together in a sentence. They may pick up on what the words mean, too. These patterns give us clues about how the model works.

We use three forms of regularization to reduce overfitting during training. We apply dropout, which randomly drops values, to each sublayer’s output before adding it to the input and normalizing the result. Dropout changes which values are available on different training passes, discouraging reliance on any one value. We also apply dropout to the combined word embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder. Position information helps the model distinguish words by their places in a sequence. In the base model, the dropout rate is $P_{drop} = 0.1$. We also use label smoothing with $\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$. This shifts some target probability from the correct answer to other possible answers. Smoothing changes the training target rather than simply choosing a different answer at test time. It makes the model less certain, which worsens perplexity, a measure of prediction quality. But it improves accuracy and the BLEU score, which measures translation quality.

We tested whether the Transformer could do a new kind of task. We asked it to show how words in an English sentence fit into groups. This task is called parsing. For instance, one group may hold a smaller group of words. A group can have a name that tells what it does in the sentence. The model must find the groups and show how they fit together. It cannot just list the words in the order they appear in the sentence. The model learns these group patterns from examples. It has to work even when there are not many examples. The answer must follow strict rules about how those groups fit together. It is also much longer than the sentence put in. With little training data, some older models have not done as well as the best models on this task. These models work by turning one sequence into another.

We tested whether the Transformer could generalize to English constituency parsing, a task outside its original domain. In this task, a model groups words into a nested structure, or parse tree, that reflects their grammatical roles. A constituent can itself contain smaller constituents, so the model must represent relations at several levels of the tree. The parse tree makes the constituent hierarchy explicit, rather than simply preserving the linear order of the sentence. A successful output must encode that hierarchy while respecting the constraints that govern how the constituents can be combined. This requires it to learn both grammatical grouping and a representation of that grouping from limited examples. The output must satisfy strong structural constraints and is much longer than the input sentence given to the model. In small-data settings, where training examples are limited, recurrent neural network sequence-to-sequence models have not achieved state-of-the-art results on this task.

To evaluate whether the Transformer can generalize to other tasks, we performed experiments on English constituency parsing. This task presents specific challenges. The representation must encode nested constituents and their grammatical relationships, which constrain the possible structures for a given sentence. In a sequence-to-sequence formulation, the model must generate a linearized representation of this hierarchy, rather than merely assign a label to the input. The structural constraints govern how constituents can be nested, while the length of the output increases the sequence the model must generate. Evaluating performance in this setting therefore involves both structural well-formedness and generalization from limited training data. The output is subject to strong structural constraints and is significantly longer than the input. Furthermore, RNN sequence-to-sequence models have not been able to attain state-of-the-art results in small-data regimes, where models must learn from relatively few available training examples while still producing a well-formed parse tree for each input sentence.

We introduced the Transformer, the first model to turn one sequence into another using attention alone. In translation, the input is a sequence of words in one language, and the output is a sequence in another. It replaces recurrent layers, which process sequences step by step, with multi-headed self-attention. This lets the model track several links within a sequence at once. Each attention head can focus on different links between words. Together, the heads help the model use context from across a sentence. For translation, the Transformer trains much faster than models built on recurrent or convolutional layers. The training speed comparison concerns how long the models take to learn, not necessarily how fast they produce translations after training. In this work, we presented the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing the recurrent layers most commonly used in encoder-decoder architectures with multi-headed self-attention. The encoder constructs representations of the source sequence, and the decoder uses those representations to generate the target sequence. In each attention head, learned projections of queries, keys and values permit the model to represent relationships among sequence positions in parallel, rather than relying on recurrent computation. For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers. The training speed comparison concerns the learning phase, while the reported benchmark results evaluate translation between English and two target languages. On both WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks, we achieve a new state of the art. In the former task our best model outperforms even all previously reported ensembles.
